newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-S&P says affirms Thailand ratings.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-S&P says affirms Thailand ratings.

text.p: Ratings agency Standard and Poor's Corp said on Tuesday it had affirmed Thailand's single-A long term and A-1 short term foreign currency debt ratings, reflecting the government's substantial financial flexibility.
S&P said the outlook remained stable but it noted heightened industry risk in the banking sector.
S&P said the ratings affected US$2.5 billion of debt outstanding.
S&P also affirmed its AA long-term local currency credit rating on Thailand's baht-denominated debt.

"While the government has ample resources to cope with potential financial sector losses, Standard and Poor's believes that the banking sector as a whole has deteriorated, affecting the ratings of all Standard and Poor's rated Thai banks," the ratings agency said.
"The ratings reflect Thailand's strong capacity to support the troubled financial sector without compromising macroeconomic stability," S&P said.

S&P said conservative fiscal management, as reflected in nine years of budget surpluses, cut the government's gross debt burden to less than four percent of gross domestic product last year, well below that of similarly rated sovereigns.

It said it recognised that rapid lending growth, particularly by finance companies to the now depressed property sector, had raised the level of problem loans, and along with it, the Thai financial sector's risk profile.
"Moreover, the government's commitment to a stable baht exchange rate means that interest rates are likely to remain high through 1997," S&P said.
As a result, the deeper than expected economic slowdown was intensifying financial pressure in the private sector.

"Asset quality in the financial system consequently should continue to deteriorate through next year, by which time interest rates may begin to decline," S&P said. "The timing and extent of any easing of credit, in turn, are critical determinants of both the magnitude of future loan losses and the extent of required government support for the financial sector."

"Reflecting a less optimistic base-case scenarios than that currently held by the Bank of Thailand, Standard and Poor's believes that official support for both creditors and borrowers could ultimately reach as much as six percent of 1997 GDP.
"This compares with support equivalent to two percent of GDP implied under the government's recently announced financial package," S&P said.
S&P said it did not expect that the likely scale of financial sector losses would seriously impair the country's credit standing.

The agency's base-case scenarios assumed little change in the Thai baht's exchange rate compared with the U.S. dollar and, continued tight credit conditions were likely at least through year-end 1997, S&P said.

"A more flexible exchange rate policy would result in easier credit and a somewhat faster pace of economic recovery than presently foreseen, albeit at the cost of exchange rate losses in the private sector.
"However, while a depreciation of the baht may impair the credit standing of some Thai borrowers with sizeable foreign currency debt, it would not adversely affect the Kingdom's ratings," S&P said.
